# Cooling the City: How Urban Design Can Tame Summer Heat

Every summer, the same pattern repeats in cities across the world: while rural areas outside the city limits swelter, the urban core registers temperatures several degrees higher. This phenomenon, the urban heat island effect, is not an accident of geography but a consequence of design. Asphalt absorbs solar radiation throughout the day and releases it slowly at night. Glass towers reflect and concentrate heat onto streets below. Air conditioners pump warm exhaust into the air while consuming electricity that strains the grid. The result is that cities, where most of humanity now lives, have become measurably hotter than they need to be—and the people who suffer most are those with the fewest resources to escape.

The good news is that heat is one of the few urban problems we know how to solve. Cities that have taken deliberate action have seen measurable results, and the toolkit is well understood: trees, thoughtful street design, better housing, and robust public transit. The challenge is not technical knowledge but political will, funding, and the honest acknowledgment that every intervention involves tradeoffs that residents must weigh.
